callout.title: Why decay is on the front page
callout.body: Every content programme quietly rots at the back while the front looks healthy. If the decay list isn't visible, the first you'll hear about it is a flat quarter eighteen months from now. It's the least flattering chart we build and the most useful.

sections.h2: Why average position isn't the headline
body: Rankings are the metric clients ask for and the metric that has aged worst. Three reasons, all structural.

First, results are personalised and localised, so there is no single position — Search Console's average position is an average across wildly different searches, and it moves when you start ranking on page four for a hundred irrelevant queries. Second, position and clicks have come apart. AI Overviews, featured snippets, video blocks and the People Also Ask stack push the first organic result further down some pages than others, so rising two places can genuinely mean fewer visits. Third, a blended average across every query you accidentally rank for is trivially gameable, and every agency knows exactly how.

So we report position per query, against a query set agreed in week one, alongside clicks for the same set. If position improves and clicks don't, that's a finding, not something to hide behind a nicer chart.

sections.h2: The baseline snapshot, frozen in week one
body: Before any work starts, we take a snapshot of all nine metrics over the trailing 90 days, write it into a document, and both sides sign it. It doesn't get revised later, which is the entire point — a baseline you can adjust is a baseline you can win against.
Two things usually complicate this, and it's better to hit them in week one than in month four.

The first is broken measurement. Plenty of Indian sites have GA4 counting a WhatsApp click as nothing, a UPI payment as an exit, and a thank-you page as three conversions. If your data can't support a baseline, we say so before we take a fee for a guarantee we can't fairly settle — see [analytics setup](/services/analytics-setup-services) for what fixing that involves.

The second is defining "qualified". A lead that leaves a phone number and a real requirement counts; a bot filling your contact form does not. We agree that definition in writing, with examples, because arguing about what counted in month three is how these promises get wriggled out of. There's a fuller walkthrough in [how to set an SEO baseline](/journal/how-to-set-an-seo-baseline).

callout.title: No baseline, no accountability
callout.body: If your current agency can't tell you what your organic lead count was on the day they started, nothing they report can be proved or disproved. That's not an oversight. It's the design.

sections.h2: The dashboard: live, read-only, yours on day one
body: The dashboard goes up during onboarding, before the first month's work is finished, and it stays live. It's built in Looker Studio on top of your own GA4, Search Console and CRM connections, so nothing sits inside our tooling where you'd need to ask us for it.
Access goes to whoever needs it, not to one nominated contact. In practice that's three people with three different questions.
bullets: **You**, checking whether leads are moving, usually on a Sunday night.
**Your finance lead**, who wants cost per organic lead next to what we invoice, and is right to want it.
**Your developer**, who needs the technical view — indexation, Core Web Vitals, crawl errors — with the affected URLs listed, not summarised.
**Read-only, always.** Nobody can quietly change a date range or drop a chart, including us. If a definition changes, it's logged on the dashboard with the date.

sections.h2: The monthly note, including the part where we were wrong
body: A dashboard tells you what happened. It cannot tell you why, and the gap between those two is where most reporting fails. So every month there's a written note, and it has four fixed parts.
It's short — usually a page — and it goes out before the review call, not during it, so the call is a conversation rather than a recital.
numbered: **What moved, and what we think caused it.** With a confidence level attached. "Impressions up 31% on the tracked set, most likely the 14 refreshed pages, though a core update landed the same week" is more useful than a clean claim we can't support.
**What didn't move.** Named. If links were flat for the second month running, it says so and explains what was in the way.

**What we got wrong.** A call that didn't work, a page that shouldn't have been written, an estimate that was optimistic. There is always something, and a note with an empty section here isn't honest.
**What happens next month**, with the two or three things we're dropping to make room.

sections.h2: What the reporting is ultimately settling
body: All of this exists to answer one question at day 90 without a debate: did the number move.

We freeze your trailing-90-day qualified leads from organic search on day one. If we haven't beaten that in 90 days, we keep working free until we do. That's the whole promise, and it only works because the measurement was agreed before there was anything at stake. We never promise a specific ranking position for a specific keyword — nobody controls Google's index, and a guarantee against a number we don't control isn't a guarantee, it's a sales line.

The uncomfortable corollary: honest reporting occasionally proves that SEO isn't your problem. If organic leads are up 40% and revenue is flat, the dashboard will show it, and the conversation moves to your sales follow-up instead of to another content plan. We'd rather have that conversation in month three than in month twelve.

faqs.q: How much do SEO reporting services cost?
faqs.a: Inside our retainers, nothing — it's included from ₹40,000/mo for smaller sites and ₹75,000/mo standard. Standalone, it's part of SEO consulting at ₹40,000 a month ex-GST. Elsewhere in India, dashboard builds are often sold as one-off projects between ₹25,000 and ₹1,00,000 depending on how many sources need connecting.

faqs.q: How often should an SEO agency report?
faqs.a: Monthly for the written read, live for the data. Weekly SEO reporting sounds diligent and mostly reports noise — Search Console data alone fluctuates enough week to week to produce a false story in either direction. If you want to check on a Tuesday, that's what the live dashboard is for.

faqs.q: What should be in a monthly SEO report?
faqs.a: Leads or revenue from organic first, then sessions to pages that sell, then conversion rate, then query-level clicks and impressions, then indexation and links. Plus a written explanation of what moved and why. If the first chart is traffic or rankings, the report is arguing rather than informing.

faqs.q: Why don't you lead with keyword rankings?
faqs.a: Because position and clicks have come apart. AI Overviews, snippets and video blocks change how far down the real first result sits, so a page can gain two positions and lose visits. We report position per query alongside clicks, so you can see when that's happening rather than being reassured by a chart.

faqs.q: Do we own the dashboard and the data?
faqs.a: Yes. It's built on your GA4, your Search Console and your CRM, and you keep all three whatever happens between us. On exit you get a full export and the dashboard file. No lock-in means nothing if the data lives in the agency's account.

faqs.q: Can you report on work another agency is doing?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's a common reason people call. That's SEO consulting at ₹40,000 a month: we build the dashboard, set the baseline, and read it each month. We won't manufacture a case against your current agency, and sometimes the honest answer is that they're doing fine.
